title: Lesson 8: Playing Progressions
intro: A progression is a sequence of chords (see Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/harmony)). Most songs use the chords of one key in a few familiar orders. This lesson shows you the chords of a key on the guitar, the number system players use, the capo, and the progressions behind thousands of songs.

items: Find the seven chords of a key and their numbers.
Play the common progressions in any key.
Use a capo to move a progression to a singer's key.
Lessons 5 (chords) and 7 (CAGED) help, but open chords are enough to start.
Step 1. Every major key has seven chords, numbered by their root's position in the scale: 1 major, 2 minor, 3 minor, 4 major, 5 major, 6 minor, 7 diminished (in Roman numerals I ii iii IV V vi vii°).
Step 2. In G major: 1 = G, 2 = Am, 3 = Bm, 4 = C, 5 = D, 6 = Em, 7 = F♯°. In C major: C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°. In D major: D, Em, F♯m, G, A, Bm, C♯°.
Step 3. Play the 1, 4, 5 and 6 chords of G: G, C, D, Em. These four make most songs in G.
Step 1. I–IV–V–I (G–C–D–G): folk, country, early rock. Strum four beats per chord.
Step 2. I–V–vi–IV (G–D–Em–C): the most common pop progression of the last few decades. Start it on the vi (Em–C–G–D) and it sounds sadder with the same chords.
Step 4. i–♭VII–♭VI–V (Am–G–F–E): the 'Andalusian' progression of flamenco and much rock; the E at the end is a major chord (G♯ in it), which pulls back to Am.
Step 5. 12-bar blues in A (A, D and E, often as seventh chords): A A A A | D D A A | E D A E. Play it with a shuffle (Step 'shuffle' below).

examples.label: 12-bar blues in A (quick run-through, half a bar per chord)
Blues shuffle on A (A5–A6 on strings 5 and 4)

items: Step 1. Session players write progressions as numbers: 1 – 5 – 6m – 4. Written this way, a progression works in any key: in G it is G – D – Em – C; in A it is A – E – F♯m – D.
Step 2. To change key without learning new shapes, use a capo. Play the G shapes with a capo at fret 2 and they sound in A; at fret 3 in B♭; at fret 5 in C.
Step 3. To fit a singer: find the key they want, then pick the open-chord key below it and capo up the difference. A song in E♭: C shapes with a capo at 3, or D shapes at 1.
4 min: G – C – D – G and G – D – Em – C, four strums per chord, no stopping at changes.
4 min: the 12-bar blues in A with the shuffle pattern.
3 min: play 1 – 5 – 6m – 4 in G, then in C, then in D with open chords.
2 min: the same in G shapes with a capo at 2 (sounding A).

blocks.title: Numbers
blocks.text: Write 1 – 5 – 6m – 4 in A major and in E♭ major.
solution: A major: A – E – F♯m – D.
E♭ major: E♭ – B♭ – Cm – A♭.

blocks.title: Capo
blocks.text: A singer wants a song in B♭. Which capo position lets you use G shapes, and which lets you use A shapes?
solution: G to B♭ is 3 semitones: capo 3 with G shapes. A to B♭ is 1 semitone: capo 1 with A shapes.

blocks.text: Sources: Goodrick, M. (1987). The Advancing Guitarist. Hal Leonard; Williams, C. (1988). The Nashville Number System. Self-published; Temperley, D. (2018). The Musical Language of Rock. Oxford University Press; Leavitt, W. G. (1966–1971). A Modern Method for Guitar, vols. 1–3. Berklee Press.
